full_judgment:
2. Plaintiff Sufia Akhter Alam (Since deceased) filed the suit for ejectment of defendant No.1 from the suit shop claiming that defendant No.1 was a defaulter. Her case is that, her mother Rijia Khatun was the owner of the suit shop and defendant No.1 was a monthly tenant under her mother since 16th June, 1964. The plaintiff further claims that her mother orally gifted the ground floor of Holding No.60/1, Purana Paltan to her on 29-8-77 and requested the monthly tenants both verbally and in writing to pay rent to the plaintiff. In pursuance to that request most of the tenants began to pay rent to the plaintiff but defendant No.1 refused to accept the plaintiff as owner and continued to deposit rent before the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No.48 of 1972 in favour of her mother. Then the plaintiff filed S.C.C. Suit No.91 of 1983 which was dismissed for default on 30-9-85. A Miscellaneous case was filed by the plaintiff which was also rejected. Then there was an attempt to settle the dispute amicably but that failed. Thereafter the plaintiff served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 8-11-87 requesting the defendant to vacate possession by 30-11-87 but the defendant did not vacate the premises. Hence the suit. 

 3. Defendant No.2, the mother of the plaintiff appeared in the suit by filing written statement and supported the case of the plaintiff by admitting that she gifted the suit shop to the plaintiff. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations. Defendant No. 1's case is that no notice of attornment was served upon him either by the plaintiff or by her mother, rather her mother continued to withdraw the amount of rent which he deposited in the court of the Rent Controller. He further claims that in 1973 Rijia Khatoon demanded rent at an exorbitant rate from him and as such he started depositing rent before the House Rent Controller by filing House Rent Control Case No. 48 of 1973. Rijia Khatoon withdrew the house rent deposited before the House Rent Controller for the last time in December, 1986. Defendant No.1 further claims that as the plaintiff could not produce any legal proof that she got the suit shop from her mother on the basis of oral gift, in spite of her claim and demand, the defendant did not pay any rent to her and he continued to deposit the rent before the House Rent Controller in favour of her mother. He also denied the relationship of the landlord and tenant and asserted that as he is depositing rent in House Rent case he is not a defaulter. 

 5. Mr S R Pal, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, submits, first, that the notice that was served under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was not sufficient as there was a specific provision in the original agreement of tenancy with the original owner, the mother of the plaintiff, for giving one month's notice to determine the tenancy and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division wrongly held that the notice that was served on the petitioner terminating the tenancy was a valid notice. The learned Advocate next submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division wrongly held that the defendant had knowledge of the change of ownership by way of oral gift from the original owner to the plaintiff and in spite of that knowledge he did not pay rent to the plaintiff and deposited rent in the House Rent case in the name of the original owner and, as such, he was a defaulter. 

 6. With regard to the first submission of Mr. SR Pal it may be stated that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was dated 8-11-87 and the same was served on 9-11-87 on the defendant terminating the tenancy with the expiry of 30-11-87 and consequently 15 days notice as contemplated under the law was given in the instant case. It is true that in the original agreement of tenancy with the plaintiffs mother there was a clause of serving of one month's notice to determine the tenancy but in the meanwhile by virtue of the oral gift the ownership of the suit shop has been transferred to the plaintiff and, as such, the question of giving one month notice as per the old lease agreement between the defendant and the original land lady does not arise. In that view of the matter the notice that was served by the plaintiff on defendant No.1 was valid and sufficient Apart from this, the defendant denied the title of the plaintiff. In the case of Muhammad Islam Khan vs. Cantonment Board reported in 1982 Supreme Court Monthly Review 1956, it has been held that the defendant's denial of the plaintiff's title without any valid reason may operate as forfeiture and in such a case notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act may be dispensed with. Further, the High Court Division found that the original tenancy came to an end in 1970 when defendant No.1 created a new partnership firm, Greenland & Co. and thus the obligation of serving one month's notice was not in force. 

 7. With regard to the contention of the learned Advocate it may be stated that both the trial Court and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found on consideration of the entire evidence on record, both oral and documentary, that defendant No.1 had full knowledge of the change of ownership. There being valid notice of attornment on the defendant orally and by written notice, defendant No.1 is a defaulter as he did not pay rent to the plaintiff, instead deposited rent in the name of original owner in the House Rent Case. This finding of fact having been accepted by the learned Single Judge, we do not like to interfere with the said finding of fact as the same is based on evidence and there is no perversity or illegality in affirming such finding of fact. The learned Single Judge rightly affirmed the decision of the trial Court and decreed the suit.
